title: Lord of the Sabbath, Greater Than Jonah
summary: Two Sabbath disputes, over picking grain and healing a withered hand, lead the Pharisees to plot Jesus' death. Matthew presents Jesus as Isaiah's gentle Servant. When the Pharisees say he casts out demons by Beelzebul, Jesus warns against blasphemy against the Spirit, refuses them any sign but Jonah's, and declares that those who do the Father's will are his true family.
story: Chapter 11 ended with Jesus' invitation to rest under his easy yoke. Chapter 12 begins, almost at once, with a fight about the day of rest itself. The rejection that chapter 11 described now hardens into open conflict, and for the first time Matthew says the Pharisees plotted how to kill Jesus (verse 14). The charge that Jesus works by the power of the prince of demons, first voiced in 9:34, is now answered at length. By the end of the chapter lines are drawn: those who oppose him, a generation that demands signs, and a new family made up of those who do the Father's will. That division sets up the parables of chapter 13, which explain why the kingdom is received by some and refused by others.
historical:
The Sabbath, the seventh day, was a central sign of Israel's covenant with God (Exodus 31:13-17), and in the centuries before Jesus it had become a mark of Jewish identity under pressure from foreign rulers. Faithful Jews had even died rather than fight on the Sabbath during the Maccabean revolt in the 160s BC (1 Maccabees 2:29-41). Jewish teachers therefore worked hard to define what counted as forbidden work. The Mishnah, compiled around AD 200 but drawing on earlier debates, lists thirty-nine main categories of work, including reaping and threshing. The Law allowed a hungry traveler to pick grain by hand from a neighbor's field (Deuteronomy 23:25); the Pharisees' objection was about doing it on the Sabbath. Many teachers also agreed that saving a life overrode the Sabbath, but a withered hand was not an emergency.

Jesus' answers draw on Scripture: David eating the consecrated bread when he fled from Saul (1 Samuel 21:1-6), and the priests, whose Sabbath offerings required work in the temple (Numbers 28:9-10). Jewish exorcists were known in this period; Josephus tells of a Jewish man named Eleazar who drove out a demon in the presence of the future emperor Vespasian. That is the background to Jesus' question about the Pharisees' own sons (verse 27). Mark 2:23-3:30 and Luke 6:1-11 and 11:14-32 contain much of this chapter's material.
cultural:
Beelzebul was a name for the ruler of demons. It is probably related to Baal-zebub, the god of the Philistine city of Ekron in 2 Kings 1:2, whose name means lord of flies; Beelzebul may mean lord of the dwelling or exalted lord, a play that fits Jesus' reply about a house and its master. Calling someone's power demonic was a serious charge, since sorcery was punishable under the law. The consecrated bread (the bread of the Presence) was twelve loaves set out each Sabbath before the Lord in the tabernacle and later the temple, and eaten afterward only by the priests (Leviticus 24:5-9).

The Queen of the South is the queen of Sheba, a kingdom in southern Arabia, who traveled to hear Solomon's wisdom (1 Kings 10). The Ninevites were the people of the Assyrian capital, Israel's bitter enemies, who repented when Jonah preached. Jesus names two Gentile examples to shame his own generation. In Jewish reckoning, part of a day could count as a whole day, so three days and three nights (verse 40) could describe a period running from Friday afternoon to Sunday morning. Family loyalty was one of the strongest bonds in the ancient world, which makes Jesus' redefinition of his family in verses 48 to 50 startling.
literary: The chapter alternates conflict and interpretation. Two Sabbath controversies (verses 1 to 14) end in a death plot. Matthew then pauses the action with the longest Old Testament quotation in his Gospel, Isaiah 42:1-4 (verses 18 to 21), which shows the kind of Messiah Jesus is: not a brawler but one who will not break a bruised reed. Then the Beelzebul controversy (verses 22 to 37) and the demand for a sign (verses 38 to 45) bring the conflict to a head. The phrase “something greater” (or one greater) runs through the chapter: greater than the temple (verse 6), than Jonah (verse 41), and than Solomon (verse 42), covering priest, prophet, and king. The closing scene about Jesus' family (verses 46 to 50) turns the chapter's question from who opposes him to who belongs to him.

outline.t: Grain picked on the Sabbath: Lord of the Sabbath
A withered hand healed; the plot to kill Jesus
The Beelzebul accusation and the strong man bound
Blasphemy against the Spirit; words and the heart
The sign of Jonah and the returning spirit

doctrines.note: Jesus does not abolish the Sabbath but interprets it by God's purpose: mercy, rest, and doing good. As Lord of the Sabbath he claims authority over the law's meaning, and he reads it through Hosea 6:6, “I desire mercy, not sacrifice.”

Jesus drives out demons by the Spirit of God, and that is the sign that God's kingdom has arrived (verse 28). To call the Spirit's work demonic, knowingly and persistently, is to reject the very means by which God forgives.
The kingdom comes as an invasion: Jesus binds the strong man and plunders his house. Satan's hold on people is being broken, which leaves no neutral ground: “He who is not with Me is against Me.”

Jesus defines his family as those who do the will of his Father. This does not reject his natural family (they appear again among believers in Acts 1:14) but establishes a new household, the church, bound by obedience to God.

words.note: Sabbaton, Sabbath, from the Hebrew shabbat, related to the verb for ceasing or resting. The day recalled God's rest after creation and Israel's release from slavery. Jesus' disputes are not about whether to keep it but about what keeping it means.

Blasphemia, slander or blasphemy, speech that insults or dishonors. Against people it means slander; against God it means speaking of him falsely or with contempt. In verses 31 and 32 it names the Pharisees' act of attributing the Spirit's work to Satan.

Semeion, sign, a token or proof that points beyond itself. The Pharisees want a sign on demand as proof, after Jesus has already healed the blind and mute. He refuses, offering only the sign of Jonah, which points to his own death and resurrection.

Pais, child or servant. In verse 18 it translates Isaiah's servant of the Lord. The same word was used for the centurion's servant in 8:6. Matthew identifies Jesus with the Servant on whom God puts his Spirit and who brings justice to the nations.

christ: The chapter piles up claims about Jesus that go beyond any prophet's. He is greater than the temple where God dwelt, Lord of the Sabbath that God instituted, greater than Jonah and Solomon, the stronger one who binds Satan, and the Servant of Isaiah 42 on whom God has put his Spirit. Yet the Servant's way is quiet: he will not break a bruised reed or snuff out a smoldering wick, and in his name the nations will put their hope. The sign of Jonah is the clearest prediction of his resurrection so far in Matthew. As Jonah was swallowed and returned, so the Son of Man will be three days in the heart of the earth, and that event, not a sign produced on demand, will be God's answer to his accusers.

hard.q: What is the blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, and can someone commit it without knowing?
hard.a:
Jesus says every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven except blasphemy against the Spirit. In context, the Pharisees have watched a man healed by the Spirit of God and declared it the work of the devil. Most interpreters take the unforgivable sin to be this kind of settled, deliberate rejection of God's evident work, calling light darkness so persistently that one refuses the only source of forgiveness. It is unforgivable not because God's mercy runs out but because the person has shut the door to it. Speaking against the Son of Man can be forgiven, perhaps because his identity was still veiled and could be misunderstood, whereas the Spirit's work in freeing the possessed was plain.

Christian pastors have long noted a practical point: people who fear they have committed this sin show by their fear that they have not, since the sin Jesus describes is marked by hardness, not by anxiety about offending God. Traditions differ on details. Some emphasize that it can only be committed by those who witnessed Jesus' works in person; others see it as final impenitence, persisting in unbelief until death. All agree that the passage is a warning to the hardened, not a threat to the troubled.

questions: Jesus reads the Sabbath through the lens of mercy. What religious habits of yours might have lost sight of their purpose?
The Servant does not break the bruised reed. Where are you bruised, and how does this picture of Jesus meet you there?
Jesus says those who do his Father's will are his family. How does belonging to that family shape how you treat other believers?
